questions.stem: Which set exactly matches the instructor's seven named digestive functions?

choices.text: Ingestion, mechanical processing, chemical digestion, secretion, absorption, compaction, defecation
Ingestion, propulsion, emulsification, filtration, absorption, excretion, elimination
Ingestion, mechanical digestion, chemical digestion, secretion, motility, absorption, digestion
Ingestion, mastication, swallowing, peristalsis, segmentation, fermentation, defecation

questions.explanation: The Chapter 24 slides count compaction among the seven; motility remains important but is not a separate item in that particular list.

questions.stem: Chewing food into smaller pieces without changing its molecular composition is an example of what?
questions.explanation: Mastication physically increases exposed surface; chemical digestion requires breaking chemical bonds.

questions.stem: Which process involves crossing the intestinal epithelial barrier into blood or lymph?
questions.explanation: Digested nutrients are not yet part of the body's internal transport systems until they cross the absorptive epithelium.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly follows food through the alimentary canal?

choices.text: Mouth, pharynx, esophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine
Mouth, pharynx, stomach, esophagus, small intestine, large intestine
Mouth, esophagus, stomach, large intestine, small intestine, anus
Mouth, pharynx, esophagus, stomach, ileum, duodenum, colon

questions.explanation: The GI tract is the continuous lumen from mouth to anus; liver, pancreas, and gallbladder are accessory organs.

questions.stem: Which organ is accessory rather than part of the tube through which food passes?
questions.explanation: Pancreatic enzymes enter the duodenum through ducts; food does not normally pass through the pancreas.

questions.stem: A moist, chewed mass swallowed from the mouth is called what?
questions.explanation: A bolus is formed in the mouth; chyme is the semifluid product of stomach mixing.

questions.stem: A stomach's partially digested, semi-fluid mixture is called what?
questions.explanation: Gastric mixing converts food and secretions into chyme before gradual release through the pylorus.

questions.stem: The synthesis of glycogen from glucose is an example of what?
questions.explanation: Anabolism builds larger molecules from smaller precursors, unlike digestion-associated catabolism.

questions.stem: Which named function concentrates waste primarily through water removal?
questions.explanation: The large intestine reabsorbs water, contributing to fecal compaction.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes chemical digestion?

choices.text: Enzymes break macromolecules into smaller digestion products
Contractions physically fragment food without bond cleavage
Enzymes transfer absorbed nutrients from portal blood into liver

questions.explanation: Chemical digestion is molecular breakdown, distinct from motility and epithelial absorption.

questions.stem: From the digestive lumen outward, which is the usual sequence of major GI wall layers?

choices.text: Mucosa, submucosa, muscularis externa, serosa or adventitia

questions.explanation: The mucosa contacts lumen contents, followed by connective submucosa, muscularis externa, then outer covering.

questions.stem: Which enteric plexus is situated between the layers of the muscularis externa and principally regulates motility?
questions.explanation: The myenteric (Auerbach) plexus lies between circular and longitudinal muscle.

questions.stem: Which GI wall plexus has an especially important role in secretion and local blood-flow regulation?

choices.text: Enteric ganglia between circular and longitudinal muscle

questions.explanation: The submucosal (Meissner) plexus resides within the submucosa.

questions.stem: Which activity primarily propels material forward along the GI tract?
questions.explanation: Propagating muscular waves produce net propulsion; segmentation chiefly mixes intestinal contents.

questions.stem: Which activity mainly mixes intestinal chyme back and forth rather than consistently pushing it toward the colon?
questions.explanation: Segmentation repeatedly exposes chyme to enzymes and absorptive epithelium.

questions.stem: How do mass movements differ from ordinary small-intestinal segmentation?

choices.text: They move colonic contents long distances toward the rectum
They repeatedly mix small-intestinal chyme in place without net propulsion
They are local mixing contractions of colonic haustra rather than long-range movement
They primarily move material from jejunum to ileum in short alternating segments

questions.explanation: Mass movements are powerful, infrequent colonic propulsive events.

questions.stem: What is the principal anatomical function of a mesentery?

choices.text: Suspend organs while carrying vessels, nerves, and lymphatics
Form the absorptive lining of small-intestinal villi
Create the smooth muscle layers of the stomach
Secrete bicarbonate into the duodenal lumen

questions.explanation: Mesenteries are double sheets of peritoneum supporting abdominal organs.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes visceral from parietal peritoneum?

choices.text: Visceral covers organs; parietal lines the body wall
Visceral lines the body wall; parietal covers organs
Both line the abdominal body wall and neither covers an organ surface
Visceral peritoneum lines the diaphragm only; parietal peritoneum covers the stomach

questions.explanation: The naming distinguishes the organ-facing covering from the cavity's wall lining.

questions.stem: Which structure is classically retroperitoneal over most of its length?
questions.explanation: Most of the pancreas lies behind the parietal peritoneum, although the tail has distinct peritoneal relationships.

questions.stem: Which outer GI layer helps anchor the thoracic esophagus to surrounding tissues?
questions.explanation: Most of the esophagus has adventitia, not a complete peritoneal serosal covering.

questions.stem: Which enzyme begins starch digestion in the mouth?
questions.explanation: Salivary amylase starts carbohydrate hydrolysis before swallowing.

questions.stem: Which salivary component contributes directly to lubrication and bolus formation?
questions.explanation: Mucins are glycoproteins that make saliva slippery and cohesive.

questions.stem: Which gland empties into the oral cavity through Stensen's duct?
questions.explanation: Stensen's (parotid) duct conducts secretion from the parotid gland.

questions.stem: Which named duct drains the submandibular gland?
questions.explanation: Wharton's duct opens on the floor of the mouth near the lingual frenulum.

questions.stem: What is the fauces?

choices.text: Opening between oral cavity and oropharynx
Opening between nasopharynx and middle ear
Junction of hard and soft palates

questions.explanation: The fauces is the mouth-to-throat opening.

questions.stem: Which tooth tissue covers the crown and is especially highly mineralized?
questions.explanation: Enamel is the hard protective covering of a tooth's crown.

questions.stem: What connects the tooth root to the surrounding alveolar bone?

choices.text: The gingival epithelium that lines the tooth neck
Cementum alone, without any connective-tissue attachment

questions.explanation: Periodontal ligament fibers attach to cementum and alveolar bone.

questions.stem: Through which root-tip opening do vessels and nerves enter a tooth?
questions.explanation: The apical foramen leads into root canal/pulp structures.

questions.stem: Which tooth group is particularly specialized for cutting food?
questions.explanation: Incisors have cutting edges, whereas canines tear and posterior teeth crush or grind.

questions.stem: The lecturer's anatomical term 'superior labium' refers to which structure?
questions.explanation: Superior and inferior labium are anatomical terms for upper and lower lip.

questions.stem: Which swallowing phase is typically under voluntary control?

choices.text: All three phases are wholly voluntary

questions.explanation: The tongue initiates swallowing voluntarily; subsequent reflex phases are coordinated involuntarily.

questions.stem: Which brainstem region is especially involved in coordinating swallowing?
questions.explanation: Brainstem swallowing circuits are centered in medullary networks.

questions.stem: What is a major protective event during the pharyngeal phase?

choices.text: The larynx elevates and the airway closes
The soft palate closes the nasopharynx while the laryngeal inlet remains open
The true vocal folds abduct widely to allow the bolus to pass
The upper esophageal sphincter stays tightly contracted as the bolus enters

questions.explanation: Multiple coordinated movements protect the airway during passage through the pharynx.

questions.stem: How does a swallowed bolus normally move down the esophagus?

choices.text: Through repeated contractions of the pyloric sphincter

questions.explanation: Esophageal peristalsis provides propulsion even when the person is not upright.

questions.stem: Which sphincter helps prevent reflux of acidic gastric contents into the esophagus?
questions.explanation: The lower esophageal high-pressure zone helps resist reflux at the stomach-esophagus junction.

questions.stem: Which pharyngeal region normally carries air but not swallowed food?
questions.explanation: The nasopharynx is an air passage; swallowed material passes through lower pharyngeal regions.

questions.stem: The opening through the diaphragm used by the esophagus is called what?
questions.explanation: The esophageal hiatus allows the esophagus to pass through the diaphragm.

questions.stem: Which statement about the epiglottis is most accurate?

choices.text: It assists airway protection along with laryngeal closure mechanisms
It is the sole structure that prevents aspiration
It opens the upper esophageal sphincter by secretion
It is the major muscle that propels the esophageal bolus

questions.explanation: Airway protection involves several coordinated laryngeal movements, not just a passive epiglottic lid.

questions.stem: Which stomach cell secretes both hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor?
questions.explanation: Parietal cells produce HCl and intrinsic factor; chief cells release pepsinogen and gastric lipase.

questions.stem: Which gastric secretion is released in an inactive form and later activated by acid?
questions.explanation: Pepsinogen is the zymogen precursor of pepsin; secreting it inactive helps protect the producing cells.

questions.stem: Which stomach cell directly secretes the precursor of pepsin?
questions.explanation: Chief cells release pepsinogen, which becomes the active protease pepsin under acidic conditions.

questions.stem: Which stomach region leads directly into the duodenum?
questions.explanation: The pyloric region includes the outlet regulated by the pyloric sphincter.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of stomach rugae?

choices.text: Allow the stomach lining to expand as it fills
Provide villus-like folds for nutrient absorption in the stomach
Prevent the gastric wall from expanding during a meal
Act as a muscular valve at the pyloric outlet

questions.explanation: Rugae are temporary folds that flatten during gastric distension.

questions.stem: Which stomach muscle arrangement helps create powerful churning?

choices.text: A third layer of striated skeletal muscle throughout the wall
Loss of the inner circular layer
Only the outer longitudinal layer contracting independently

questions.explanation: The stomach has an extra oblique muscular layer in addition to the usual circular and longitudinal layers.

questions.stem: Why does gastric acid not normally destroy the stomach epithelium?

choices.text: A mucus-bicarbonate barrier and epithelial defenses limit acid injury
Bicarbonate neutralizes all acid throughout the stomach lumen
Pepsin remains completely inactive in the acidic stomach
The stomach lining relies on rapid absorption of acid into portal blood

questions.explanation: Mucus, bicarbonate, tight barriers, blood flow, and repair protect the gastric lining.

questions.stem: If intrinsic factor secretion fails, which nutrient's absorption is especially impaired?
questions.explanation: Intrinsic factor enables efficient B12 uptake in the terminal ileum.

questions.stem: Which protein-digesting enzyme works in the highly acidic stomach?
questions.explanation: Pepsin is active in gastric acid and begins substantial protein digestion.

questions.stem: Which cell type secretes gastrin?
questions.explanation: G cells are gastric enteroendocrine cells; gastrin generally stimulates gastric secretory activity.

questions.stem: Why can the thought or smell of food stimulate gastric secretion before a meal?

choices.text: Cephalic-phase vagal signaling prepares the stomach
A stomach stretch reflex is triggered before food reaches the stomach
Olfactory receptors release gastrin directly into the bloodstream
Duodenal CCK is released solely in response to the smell of food

questions.explanation: Sensory cues can activate brainstem-vagal pathways during the cephalic phase.

questions.stem: A meal stretches the stomach and introduces peptides. Which regulatory phase predominates?
questions.explanation: Distension and luminal peptides stimulate gastric-phase signaling and secretion.

questions.stem: What typically happens when acidic, fatty chyme begins entering the duodenum?

choices.text: Gastric secretion and emptying are slowed
Gastric secretion and emptying both accelerate sharply
The pyloric sphincter loses all regulatory tone

questions.explanation: Enterogastric feedback limits delivery until the small intestine can process the incoming chyme.

questions.stem: Which reflex can promote movement from the terminal ileum toward the cecum when the stomach becomes active?
questions.explanation: The gastroileal reflex helps coordinate upper-GI activity with distal intestinal movement.

questions.stem: Which two types of signal most directly integrate gastric regulation across the cephalic, gastric, and intestinal phases?

choices.text: Only circulating dietary glucose without neurons
Only motor output from the spinal cord

questions.explanation: Gastric phases reflect integrated CNS, enteric, and hormonal signals.

questions.stem: Which hormone is most strongly associated with gastric acid stimulation?
questions.explanation: Gastrin from G cells promotes gastric acid secretion; secretin and somatostatin tend to inhibit gastric activity.

questions.stem: Which intestinal hormone is especially triggered by acidic chyme and stimulates pancreatic bicarbonate secretion?
questions.explanation: S cells respond to acid by releasing secretin, helping neutralize duodenal contents.

questions.stem: A fatty meal enters the duodenum. Which hormone drives gallbladder contraction and pancreatic enzyme secretion?
questions.explanation: CCK is released by I cells in response to fats and proteins.

questions.stem: Which hormone from D cells inhibits gastrin and gastric acid secretion?
questions.explanation: Somatostatin provides inhibitory feedback in gastric regulation.

questions.stem: Which hormone is released by intestinal K cells and supports glucose-dependent insulin secretion?
questions.explanation: GIP is an incretin hormone; it is not a digestive enzyme.

questions.stem: Which signaling substance is particularly associated with intestinal vasodilation?
questions.explanation: VIP is an enteric neuropeptide, rather than a classic gland-produced digestive enzyme.

questions.stem: Which hormone-cell pairing is correct?
questions.explanation: Duodenal S cells release secretin in response to acid; other hormone-cell assignments shown are mismatched.

questions.stem: Which hormone-cell pairing is correct for CCK production?
questions.explanation: I cells in the small intestine release CCK after exposure to fats and proteins.

questions.stem: What is the most appropriate immediate response to excess acid arriving in the duodenum?

choices.text: Increase bicarbonate delivery while restraining gastric emptying
Increase gastrin release while reducing pancreatic bicarbonate secretion
Accelerate gastric emptying to deliver more acid to the duodenum
Increase pancreatic protease secretion while inhibiting ductal bicarbonate release

questions.explanation: Secretin promotes bicarbonate and enterogastric feedback helps slow continued acid delivery.

questions.stem: Which small-intestinal section first receives both pancreatic secretion and bile?
questions.explanation: The duodenum is the principal mixing site for acidic chyme, pancreatic juice, and bile.

questions.stem: Which section typically accounts for the bulk of nutrient absorption?
questions.explanation: The jejunum has extensive absorptive surface and is a major site of nutrient uptake.

questions.stem: Which segment is especially important for vitamin B12-intrinsic factor uptake and bile-salt recovery?
questions.explanation: The terminal ileum absorbs B12 bound to intrinsic factor and reclaims bile salts.

questions.stem: Which structural sequence goes from larger folds to smaller surface specializations?
questions.explanation: Plicae are larger folds, villi are mucosal projections, and microvilli are microscopic enterocyte membrane projections.

questions.stem: What is a lacteal?

choices.text: Lymphatic capillary within an intestinal villus
Blood capillary inside an intestinal villus
Lymphoid follicle within an intestinal Peyer patch
Venous channel that drains directly into the hepatic portal vein

questions.explanation: Lacteals receive chylomicron-rich lymph after fat absorption.

questions.stem: Which pathway correctly describes most absorbed long-chain dietary fat leaving the intestine?

choices.text: Enterocyte, chylomicron, lacteal, lymph, systemic blood
Enterocyte, portal capillary, hepatic portal vein, liver
Enterocyte, bile duct, gallbladder, common bile duct

questions.explanation: Long-chain dietary lipids are packaged as chylomicrons and enter lymph before systemic blood.

questions.stem: Most absorbed monosaccharides and amino acids initially reach which organ through the hepatic portal circulation?
questions.explanation: Portal venous drainage carries many water-soluble digestion products to the liver first.

questions.stem: Which specialized intestinal cell contributes to innate defense by releasing antimicrobial products?
questions.explanation: Paneth cells at intestinal crypt bases secrete lysozyme and antimicrobial peptides.

questions.stem: Where are Peyer's patches especially prominent?
questions.explanation: Peyer's patches are aggregated intestinal lymphoid tissues associated with immune surveillance.

questions.stem: Which structure releases alkaline mucus in the proximal duodenum?
questions.explanation: Brunner's glands lie in the duodenal submucosa and help protect against acid.

questions.stem: What is the brush border?

choices.text: Microvillus-rich surface of enterocytes bearing terminal digestive enzymes
Mucus-rich coating lying above the intestinal villi
Circular folds formed by the intestinal mucosa and submucosa
The capillary network running through the center of each villus

questions.explanation: Brush border microvilli expand membrane area and carry disaccharidases and other enzymes.

questions.stem: Which part of the pancreas lies in the C-shaped curve of the duodenum?
questions.explanation: The pancreatic head fits against the duodenal C-loop.

questions.stem: Which pancreatic tissue produces digestive enzymes released into ducts?
questions.explanation: The pancreas is mixed endocrine and exocrine; acini are its enzyme-producing exocrine units.

questions.stem: Which pancreatic secretion chemically helps neutralize incoming acidic chyme?
questions.explanation: Pancreatic duct cells supply bicarbonate to raise duodenal pH.

questions.stem: Which enzyme family is responsible for pancreatic protein digestion?
questions.explanation: Trypsin and other pancreatic proteases digest proteins, while amylase acts on starch and lipase on fats.

questions.stem: Which pancreatic enzyme principally breaks down triglycerides?
questions.explanation: Lipase performs triglyceride hydrolysis; bile salts help emulsify lipids but are not enzymes.

questions.stem: Why are many pancreatic proteases secreted as inactive precursors?

choices.text: To limit self-digestion of pancreatic tissue
Delay their activation until they have entered the bloodstream
Keep protein digestion restricted to the acidic stomach
Prevent bicarbonate from reacting with pancreatic enzymes

questions.explanation: Zymogen secretion helps prevent premature activation of damaging proteases inside the pancreas.

questions.stem: Which duct is also called the duct of Wirsung?
questions.explanation: The main pancreatic duct conveys exocrine pancreatic secretions toward the duodenum.

questions.stem: Which organ's endocrine tissue contains insulin-secreting islets?
questions.explanation: Pancreatic islets release hormones to blood, distinct from acini that send enzymes into ducts.

questions.stem: Which liver cell performs much of the liver's metabolic work and produces bile?
questions.explanation: Hepatocytes handle metabolism and synthesis; Kupffer cells are resident macrophages.

questions.stem: What is the primary role of Kupffer cells?

choices.text: Macrophage-based immune surveillance and particle removal
Synthesis of bile acids by liver parenchymal cells
Storage and concentration of bile before a meal
Support and organization of hepatic plates and sinusoids

questions.explanation: Kupffer cells are specialized hepatic macrophages lining sinusoids.

questions.stem: Which organ produces bile?
questions.explanation: Hepatocytes make bile; the gallbladder stores and concentrates it.

questions.stem: Which description of bile is correct?

choices.text: It emulsifies dietary fats but contains no digestive enzymes
It is produced by the gastric chief cells
It enters the mouth through Stensen's duct

questions.explanation: Bile salts disperse fat droplets and aid micelles; digestive lipases provide fat-hydrolyzing enzyme activity.

questions.stem: Which two ducts unite to form the common hepatic duct?

choices.text: Right hepatic duct and left hepatic duct
Common hepatic duct and cystic duct
Common bile duct and main pancreatic duct
Cystic duct and accessory pancreatic duct

questions.explanation: Bile leaving the right and left sides of liver converges in the common hepatic duct.

questions.stem: Which ducts unite to form the common bile duct?

choices.text: Common hepatic duct and cystic duct
Right hepatic duct and left hepatic duct
Common bile duct and main pancreatic duct
Accessory pancreatic duct and cystic duct

questions.explanation: The cystic duct connects gallbladder outflow to the common hepatic duct.

questions.stem: During gallbladder contraction, which route carries bile toward the intestine?

choices.text: Cystic duct, common bile duct, duodenum
Gallbladder, common hepatic duct, cystic duct, duodenum
Gallbladder, cystic duct, common hepatic duct, stomach
Gallbladder, cystic duct, portal vein, duodenum

questions.explanation: Bile exits gallbladder via cystic duct and continues in the common bile duct toward the duodenum.

questions.stem: Which hormone stimulates gallbladder contraction following a fatty meal?
questions.explanation: Intestinal CCK responds to fats and proteins to coordinate enzyme and bile delivery.

questions.stem: Where are most bile salts recovered for reuse?
questions.explanation: The enterohepatic cycle retrieves bile salts from the ileum back to the liver through portal blood.

questions.stem: Which sphincter regulates bile and pancreatic-fluid entry into the duodenum?
questions.explanation: The hepatopancreatic sphincter surrounds the distal biliary-pancreatic outflow region.

questions.stem: Which lobe is identified on the liver's inferior surface close to the gallbladder fossa?
questions.explanation: Quadrate and caudate are anatomical liver lobes identified on the visceral surface.

questions.stem: What does the round ligament of the liver represent developmentally?

choices.text: Remnant of the fetal umbilical vein
Remnant of the fetal ductus venosus
Remnant of the fetal umbilical artery
Remnant of the embryonic common bile duct

questions.explanation: The ligamentum teres hepatis is a fibrous remnant associated with fetal umbilical circulation.

questions.stem: Which is a major function of the large intestine?

choices.text: Absorption of most dietary amino acids

questions.explanation: The colon recovers water and electrolytes and stores waste; most nutrient absorption occurs earlier.

questions.stem: What are haustra?
questions.explanation: Haustra are colon pouches, unlike small-intestinal villi or stomach rugae.

questions.stem: What are taeniae coli?

choices.text: Longitudinal smooth-muscle bands of the colon

questions.explanation: Three longitudinal muscle bands contribute to the colon's sacculated appearance.

questions.stem: Which colon bend lies nearest the liver?
questions.explanation: The hepatic flexure joins ascending and transverse colon on the right side.

questions.stem: Which sequence follows the colon from its right side toward rectum?
questions.explanation: The colon traverses right, across, left, then curves through sigmoid into rectum.

questions.stem: What initiates the defecation reflex?

choices.text: Release of pepsin by chief cells
A rise in salivary pH alone
Arrival of chyme in the duodenum

questions.explanation: Fecal filling stretches the rectum and activates enteric and spinal pathways.

questions.stem: Which anal sphincter is primarily involuntary smooth muscle?
questions.explanation: The internal sphincter is smooth muscle; the external sphincter is skeletal muscle under voluntary control.

questions.stem: Why can some dietary fiber contribute energy despite resisting human digestive enzymes?

choices.text: Colonic microbes ferment it into absorbable short-chain fatty acids
Salivary amylase digests all fiber to glucose
The gallbladder converts fiber directly to fat
Gastric acid turns it into amino acids

questions.explanation: Microbial fermentation in the colon produces acetate, propionate, and butyrate.

questions.stem: Which structure is the first blind pouch of the large intestine?
questions.explanation: The ileocecal junction empties into the cecum.

questions.stem: Which structure is correctly paired with the spleen as an adjacent landmark?
questions.explanation: The splenic flexure lies between transverse and descending colon near the spleen.

questions.stem: Which condition involves inflammation of the pancreas?
questions.explanation: Pancreatitis refers to pancreatic inflammation, sometimes associated with obstruction by gallstones.

questions.stem: Which condition commonly reflects backflow of acidic stomach contents into the esophagus?
questions.explanation: Lower esophageal sphincter dysfunction can contribute to reflux symptoms such as heartburn.

questions.stem: Which condition denotes inflammation of the stomach mucosa?
questions.explanation: Gastritis is stomach inflammation, distinct from liver or colonic inflammation.

questions.stem: Which condition describes chronic advanced liver scarring with architectural distortion?
questions.explanation: Cirrhosis represents advanced fibrosis and tissue remodeling following chronic liver injury.

questions.stem: A patient develops yellowing of the skin and sclera from high bilirubin. What is the finding called?
questions.explanation: Jaundice is visible bilirubin-associated yellowing, not a specific cause.

questions.stem: Which infectious condition can cause severe watery diarrhea by promoting intestinal fluid secretion?
questions.explanation: Toxigenic Vibrio cholerae drives marked secretory fluid loss.

questions.stem: What is the definition of gingivitis?
questions.explanation: Gingivitis affects the gums; periodontal disease can involve deeper supporting structures.

questions.stem: Which condition most directly involves stone formation in the gallbladder or bile ducts?
questions.explanation: Gallstones can obstruct biliary drainage and may trigger pancreatitis.
